ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a warm, informal academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. There is frequent lightweight overlap—greetings, affirmations, laughter-like reactions, and quick acknowledgments—but speakers generally yield the floor for formal Q&A. Participants use many fillers and repairs (“um,” “yeah,” “I mean,” repeated starts), with occasional fragmented or unpolished phrasing, especially from non-native speakers. The tone is collegial and enthusiastic, relying on praise before questions and softening challenges through hedges such as “I’m curious,” “do you think,” “it could be,” and “I’m not sure.” Questions are usually prefaced with context or a compliment, then unfold as exploratory multi-part prompts rather than terse interrogations. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative interpretations, or open questions rather than confrontation. Participants build on each other by referencing a prior comment, offering related observations, and inviting future collaboration; the host provides brief procedural transitions and closes segments efficiently.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Building a wrist-worn sensor and model that flags irregular heart rhythm early enough for a clinic to follow up.

speakers.name: Priya Shah
speakers.background: A fourth-year computer science PhD student leading the machine-learning work for the pilot under a faculty advisor. She has spent three years developing time-series classifiers for photoplethysmography and inertial-sensor streams, with experience in weak supervision, calibration, distribution-shift detection, and retrospective evaluation on de-identified wearable datasets. She is responsible for the alerting model, data pipeline specifications, labeling schema, and monitoring plan.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya frames the problem as a sequential decision system operating under uncertainty: an alert threshold is a tunable operating point on a sensitivity-specificity curve, while signal-quality gating, missingness, class imbalance, label latency, and population shift determine whether offline performance transfers to prospective use. She tends to question clinically intuitive rules that are not operationalized as measurable variables and presses the group to specify endpoints, ground truth, and error costs.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: A biomedical engineering professor and device-systems investigator with 14 years of experience designing and validating ambulatory physiologic monitoring hardware. His lab has conducted studies of PPG, ECG, accelerometry, electrode-free sensing, embedded firmware, and human-factors performance in home-use devices. As principal investigator, he oversees hardware integration, verification testing, risk documentation, device logistics, and the technical evidence package for future regulatory discussions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo approaches the pilot as an end-to-end measurement-chain problem. He focuses on whether wrist placement, skin contact, optical coupling, motion artifact, firmware behavior, battery state, and on-device computation preserve a physiologically interpretable signal before any model is asked to classify it. He is attentive to verification and traceability, but is willing to alter engineering assumptions when clinical workflow or prospective data indicate that the system is not usable.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Helen Brooks
speakers.background: A cardiologist with 18 years of practice experience in outpatient arrhythmia evaluation and ambulatory-monitor interpretation, who also directs clinical operations for digital-cardiology studies at the affiliated health system. She manages referral pathways, cardiology-review procedures, clinician communication, safety escalation, and coordination with primary-care sites. Her research experience includes pragmatic prospective studies in routine-care populations and adjudication of rhythm-related outcomes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Dr. Brooks treats the device as a workflow intervention rather than merely a classifier. She distinguishes a screening alert from a diagnosis, asks whether an alert can be acted on safely and intelligibly, and prioritizes clear responsibility for follow-up, confirmatory testing, documentation, and patient communication. She is wary of technical performance claims that do not map onto clinical decision-making, referral burden, and the realities of a busy cardiology service.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

benchmark_task: Give a long meeting where an early constraint makes a later decision unworkable, and nobody connects them. Separate the two moments with substantive discussion. The evaluated AI must flag the conflict and cite both moments.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a long meeting where an early constraint makes a later decision unworkable, and nobody connects them. Separate the two moments with substantive discussion. The evaluated AI must flag the conflict and cite both moments.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction:
Simulate a long, natural planning meeting involving Priya Shah from computer science, Mateo Alvarez from biomedical engineering, Dr. Helen Brooks from clinical medicine, and a study coordinator. The meeting must begin with Dr. Brooks clearly stating an operational constraint: cardiology can review no more than 10 device-generated alerts per week during the pilot because no additional clinical staff will be funded. The coordinator should record this as a settled planning constraint. Do not discuss its implications for later alert-threshold selection.

Then include substantial intervening discussion across disciplines: signal-quality checks, motion artifact and sensor placement, participant onboarding, data labeling and model-drift monitoring, battery/on-device computation tradeoffs, regulatory evidence, and the distinction between an alert and a diagnosis. Participants may make ordinary decisions and assignments in these areas.

Later in the meeting, Priya must propose and the group must adopt a model operating threshold designed to maximize sensitivity, with a projected 25 alerts per week in the planned enrollment. Priya should state that this threshold is selected despite its false-positive rate because the pilot should avoid missed possible arrhythmias. Mateo and Dr. Brooks may agree with the sensitivity rationale, but nobody may connect the projected 25 weekly alerts to the earlier maximum capacity of 10 weekly cardiology reviews. Do not resolve, notice, soften, or mention this contradiction. End with the threshold decision and ordinary next steps, leaving the conflict unnoticed.

ground_truth.issue_type: unnoticed conflict between an early operational constraint and a later model decision

conflicting_moment_1.fact: Cardiology can review at most 10 device-generated alerts per week during the pilot, with no additional staff funding.

conflicting_moment_2.speaker: Priya Shah and meeting group
conflicting_moment_2.fact: The group adopts a sensitivity-maximizing alert threshold projected to generate 25 alerts per week at planned enrollment.

ground_truth.why_unworkable: The adopted threshold would produce 15 more alerts per week than the clinic has capacity to review. Since the device workflow depends on cardiology follow-up, the threshold decision cannot be implemented as agreed without changing staffing, enrollment, triage, or the threshold.
ground_truth.expected_evaluated_answer: Flag the conflict explicitly and cite both the 10-alerts-per-week cardiology review limit and the later 25-alerts-per-week threshold projection. Explain that the team must reconcile the alert volume with review capacity before proceeding; possible remedies may include revising the threshold, adding a triage layer or staff, limiting enrollment, or changing the follow-up workflow.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Hope you managed to stay dry getting in. Campus was pretty unpleasant this morning. Before we get too deep into the six-month pilot details, I'd like us to leave today with a clear view of what's actually ready and what still needs evidence. I mean, that includes the device configuration, the event-review workflow, and the model assumptions around imperfect home data. Priya, could you start us off with where the pipeline stands since our last discussion?

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: It was pretty grim out. On the pipeline, the prospective path is basically wired through. We have raw windows and timestamped quality and missingness metadata, then a possible-rhythm-irregularity alert, not a diagnosis, with a separate record for provisional follow-up versus eventual adjudication. The thing I don't want to hand-wave is the threshold. The sensitivity-forward setting is about 25 alerts a week at planned enrollment, and I think we should start there rather than- rather than optimize for a pretty retrospective precision number.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: Twenty-five is not operationally viable. Cardiology can review at most ten device-generated alerts a week, full stop; please put that in the operations log. Priya, can the retained event record distinguish waveform-driven alerts from motion or missingness?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, that is tight.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Yes. Each alert can carry separate provenance fields: the model score and waveform window, motion/contact-quality summaries, and missingness features, so we can tell whether it was genuinely waveform-driven versus triggered in a degraded context. But if ten is a hard cap, we need to decide explicitly whether the pilot prioritizes sensitivity under triage or whether we are changing the scientific operating point; I can’t just calibrate to a queue limit and call the resulting miss rate acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: It is not a queue limit in the abstract; it is the available clinical service, and the pilot cannot generate alerts we have no safe owner for. I’m not asking you to conceal the miss rate—quite the opposite. We need to prospectively characterize the sensitivity and the cases deferred by whatever triage rule gets us to ten, then keep feasibility, alert performance, and confirmed arrhythmia outcomes separate.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Then I’d treat ten as the actionable review stream, but we need to preserve the pre-triage candidate stream and log every suppression with its score, quality state, and reason. Otherwise we won’t know whether the apparent sensitivity is model failure or a service-capacity decision. Helen, for the ten that do reach you, does an episode-level summary with timing, duration, and signal quality actually change whether you order a reference monitor or escalate?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: That is the minimum useful packet. I need the actual strip or waveform window, the episode timing and duration, the quality and contact context, and enough context to know whether this is repeated or isolated. Then it’s usually not just monitor or not, it’s whether there’s a clinically credible signal, symptoms, or risk that warrants confirmatory ECG monitoring. A high score without an interpretable signal shouldn’t generate a patient call as if we’ve found an arrhythmia.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Yeah, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: For that packet to mean anything, I need the quality field tied back to the acquisition conditions, not just as a downstream label. I'd include battery state, firmware build, and a synchronized motion/contact trace with the strip. Otherwise, a late upload or a reconnect artifact can look like an episode-timing- actually, it can look like an episode-timing issue. Helen, would that help with your review, or is that too much operational detail on the clinical side?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: Useful, but I wouldn't put battery state and firmware detail in the clinician-facing view by default. That would obscure the strip and the quality interpretation. Keep it available in the audit record, and surface a plain acquisition-quality flag with the motion/contact context. Also, Mateo, what are you seeing with real-world wear after the first few days? Can removal, charging, or poor fit be recognized instead of read as clinically quiet time?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: In the small home-use run, removal and charging were usually inferable from the combined PPG amplitude, contact metric, and accelerometer pattern. Poor fit, though- it can look like intermittent low perfusion, so that part is less clean. The more concerning issue is that two units had repeated Bluetooth reconnects, with accelerated drain and delayed event timestamps, so I would not yet label all apparent quiet intervals as non-wear until we isolate whether that's the app, firmware retry logic, or phone settings.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: That’s exactly the confound I’m worried about. In the held-out data, several very high-confidence overnight positives had long missing stretches earlier that same day. So until we can separate non-wear and reconnect artifacts from actual behavioral or physiology-linked missingness, I don’t think we can treat missingness as a reassuring quality feature. Do you have a sense whether those two units were on the same firmware build?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: They were on the same production firmware build, though not the same phone model or OS version. I don't want to infer a firmware-wide defect from two units, but the shared build does make the retry-loop hypothesis plausible. We have the device logs, so we should compare the reconnect cadence, current draw, and local clock against the phone-side sync record before we- before we treat those missing intervals as model features.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: And until that’s resolved, a gap cannot be documented as clinically quiet. It’s just unavailable or indeterminate data. For the pilot record, I want that distinction explicit. Non-wear, suspected technical loss, and low-quality wear are different states because otherwise we’ll make rather, rather misleading claims about both adherence and negative findings.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd make those mutually exclusive acquisition states in the device data model, with an indeterminate state whenever the clock or transfer integrity is compromised. And before enrollment, I need the enclosure and strap locked for the six months, because otherwise changes in optical coupling will blur low-quality wear with, with a hardware revision.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Yeah, and that hardware lock matters for calibration too. If optical coupling shifts mid-pilot, the quality gate is no longer the one we validated, and trying to hold the actionable stream to ten reviews a week—versus the roughly 25 candidate alerts at the sensitivity-forward threshold—becomes pretty uninterpretable. I’d want firmware and enclosure/strap version carried with every window, not just every device.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: Mm-hm, that needs version control.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: The per-window provenance is essential, especially because a device-level label won't capture a firmware update, an intermittent reconnect state, or a replacement strap. I can lock the enclosure and strap for the pilot, as long as we finish the reconnect analysis before release. Otherwise we'd be freezing a configuration whose timing integrity we haven't actually verified, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: I agree, do not freeze it just because the calendar wants us to. From the clinical side, I need a go or no-go criterion on that analysis. If event timing cannot be trusted, the ten-alert-per-week review pathway is not really evaluable because we cannot tell what was available for review when. And patient-facing language has to wait until I’ve, I’ve cleared the consent and safety-escalation wording with clinical research.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I can define it in engineering terms. For every retained event, we need bounded device-to-phone timing error, no unaccounted partial-window loss, and a reconciled audit trail from acquisition through upload. I need Priya to specify the maximum jitter and window loss her calibration tolerates. Then the reconnect analysis can- then it can be a real release gate, not a qualitative judgment.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Yeah. I need to derive that from the windowing and the threshold analysis, but it cannot be just average clock drift: an unaccounted gap can change both the episode summary and whether a candidate crosses threshold. I’ll come back with tolerances for timestamp error and retained-window loss, and then we can see whether the sensitivity-forward stream—about 25 candidates a week before the ten-review triage—is even valid on that build.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Once you have those bounds, I’ll run them against the reconnect traces, rather than reporting a generic battery result. If we can’t demonstrate retained event timing and window integrity within your limits across the phone configurations we expect in the network, I would hold the release. The clinical workflow should not be asked to compensate for an unverified, unverified acquisition chain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: Good. And just so it stays unambiguous in the release criteria, the clinical pathway remains capped at ten device-generated alerts per week; anything above that is retained as a non-actioned candidate with the suppression rationale, not silently dropped. Once your timing gate and Priya’s tolerances are met, I can take the final consent and urgent-symptom language through clinical research, but I don’t want that wording finalized against a build we may hold.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Right, that sequencing is important.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: I’ll keep the release analysis separate from the endpoint definition. We still need to settle whether calibration is assessed against every returned reference monitor or only completed clinical workups. Those aren’t interchangeable, especially if suppressed candidates never get a monitor. Otherwise, the ten-review cap can make the model look calibrated just by censoring the difficult cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: We’re at time, so let’s not settle that endpoint by implication. We need to preserve the candidate denominator, record the ten-per-week clinical cap in the operations log, and prospectively track who gets a reference monitor and who doesn’t. Otherwise diagnosed-arrhythmia yield is a workflow- no, it’s a workflow outcome, not a calibration result.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: All right, we’re at the hard stop. Thank you both. We’ll pick this up once we have the timing analysis and tolerance bounds in hand.

transcript.speaker: Priya Shah
transcript.text: Thanks, bye.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Helen Brooks
transcript.text: Thank you—take care, both.
